note.question: How should sparse graphs for stochastic matching with an application to middle-mile transportation management be designed?
note.overview: Given an input graph [Formula: see text], we consider the problem of designing a sparse subgraph [Formula: see text] with [Formula: see text] that supports a large matching after some nodes in V are randomly deleted. This paper studies four families of sparse graph designs (namely, clusters, rings, chains, and Erdős–Rényi graphs) and show both theoretically and numerically that their performance is close to the optimal one achieved by a complete graph. The paper's interest in the stochastic sparse graph design problem is primarily motivated by a collaboration with a leading e-commerce retailer in the context of its middle-mile delivery operations.

source.quote: Given an input graph [Formula: see text], we consider the problem of designing a sparse subgraph [Formula: see text] with [Formula: see text] that supports a large matching after some nodes in V are randomly deleted.
Our interest in the stochastic sparse graph design problem is primarily motivated by a collaboration with a leading e-commerce retailer in the context of its middle-mile delivery operations.
This supports our model premises to focus on indirect shipping routes containing up to two stations.

The middle-mile transportation system is responsible for moving parcels from large regional warehouses to last-mile delivery stations (these correspond to the nodes V in the graph Gin), which act as transfer cen­ ters between regional warehouses and local custo­ mers.

In other words, delivery routes of the trucks are not nec­ essarily stable, creating additional complexity in the scheduling and coordination of drivers, most of whom operate as independent contractors.
To measure sparsity, we use the density d(G) of graph G as defined in Section 2.1.
